RFC 5545 recurrence must be treated as a local civil-time set when DTSTART has a TZID: generate rule candidates in that timezone, apply the RFC’s DST resolution rule, enforce each RRULE’s COUNT during generation, then union DTSTART/RRULE/RDATE and subtract EXDATE. Materialize only a bounded future window, with idempotent PostgreSQL writes keyed by the immutable original recurrence identity—not by mutable UTC time.

## RFC 5545 semantics

For a recurring VEVENT, the recurrence set is:
Duplicates in the inclusion side are collapsed; EXDATE takes precedence, including over DTSTART. EXDATE must have the same value type as DTSTART; specifically, a TZID date-time recurrence needs corresponding local/TZID exception values.

## COUNT and EXDATE

COUNT limits the output of that RRULE’s generation, not the number of visible instances after exclusions.
Example:
```
DTSTART;TZID=Europe/Paris:20261023T023000 RRULE:FREQ=DAILY;COUNT=5 EXDATE;TZID=Europe/Paris:20261025T023000
```
Correct behavior:
- The RRULE generates five nominal candidates.
- The overall recurrence set removes the excluded candidate.
- The result has four visible RRULE-derived instances—not a sixth replacement occurrence.
Do not “keep generating until five non-excluded occurrences remain.” That violates the set-construction model: inclusion sources are gathered first, exclusions are applied afterward.
Also:
- DTSTART is always the first recurrence-set member, even if it does not happen to fit the RRULE pattern; however, RFC 5545 calls the resulting recurrence set undefined when DTSTART does not match the RRULE pattern.
- UNTIL and COUNT must not occur together in one RRULE.
- An EXDATE may exclude DTSTART; retain the master event/series metadata anyway, because a cancelled first logical occurrence can still be needed for identity and later exceptions.

## DST: fold and gap rules

RFC 5545 explicitly specifies the behavior that many recurrence libraries leave to their underlying runtime:
RFC 5545’s example explains that an ambiguous 01:30 is taken as the first occurrence and a nonexistent 02:30 is interpreted with the pre-gap UTC offset. Therefore, neither “let PHP pick whatever its timezone database currently chooses” nor “shift the recurrence candidate forward to the next valid local time” is portable RFC behavior.

## Recommended canonical keys

Keep two distinct concepts:
- Recurrence identity: a normalized nominal local RECURRENCE-ID-like value, for example 2026-10-25T01:30:00|Europe/Paris, or an all-day date.
- Execution/display instant: resolved timestamptz UTC instant, calculated under your recorded tzdata/version and RFC fold/gap policy.
For a series in a timezone, do not use only starts_at_utc as the occurrence’s logical key. Rule edits, tzdata changes, explicit exception handling, and fold policy can otherwise make a previously generated logical occurrence appear to be a different one.

## Bounded materialization design

Do not expand unbounded RRULEs indefinitely. Expand only a deterministic horizon, e.g.:
and record a watermark stating through which recurrence range and which series revision expansion is complete.
A robust series record needs at least:
```
recurring_series ( id uuid primary key, timezone text not null, dtstart_local timestamp not null, rrule text null, rdates jsonb not null default '[]', exdates jsonb not null default '[]', revision bigint not null, cancelled_at timestamptz null, expansion_through_local timestamp null, expansion_revision bigint null, tzdata_version text null, updated_at timestamptz not null )
```
A materialized occurrence should preserve source identity rather than merely copying current series attributes:
```
recurring_occurrence ( id uuid primary key, series_id uuid not null references recurring_series(id), recurrence_key text not null, nominal_local timestamp null, occurrence_date date null, timezone text null, starts_at timestamptz not null, ends_at timestamptz not null, series_revision bigint not null, state text not null, -- scheduled | cancelled | overridden generated_at timestamptz not null, cancelled_at timestamptz null, unique (series_id, recurrence_key) );
```
For timed events, recurrence_key should be derived from the original local scheduled identifier, not from an override’s moved time. For all-day events, it is usually the ISO local date. For an imported iCalendar object, use a normalized RECURRENCE-ID representation consistent with the master’s DTSTART value type.

## Expansion transaction

Use a short series-scoped transaction:
```
begin; select * from recurring_series where id = :series_id for update; -- Re-read master, exclusions, explicit overrides, cancellation state. -- Generate only [from_local, to_local], applying RFC local-time policy. -- Insert candidates idempotently. insert into recurring_occurrence ( id, series_id, recurrence_key, nominal_local, timezone, starts_at, ends_at, series_revision, state, generated_at ) values (...) on conflict (series_id, recurrence_key) do update set starts_at = excluded.starts_at, ends_at = excluded.ends_at, series_revision = excluded.series_revision, generated_at = excluded.generated_at where recurring_occurrence.state = 'scheduled' and recurring_occurrence.series_revision < excluded.series_revision; update recurring_series set expansion_through_local = greatest( coalesce(expansion_through_local, '-infinity'::timestamp), :to_local ), expansion_revision = revision where id = :series_id; commit;
```
The row lock makes “read definition → generate → insert/upsert → advance watermark” one serialized operation per series. The unique constraint is still mandatory: it is the final idempotency barrier if a job is retried, a lock discipline is bypassed, or a recovery path overlaps.
At PostgreSQL’s default READ COMMITTED, INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE guarantees that each proposed row will either insert or update, even if a conflicting transaction was not visible at statement start. That makes it a good fit for idempotent occurrence writes.

## Cancellation and edits

Use cancellation as state, not destructive deletion.
A watermark alone is insufficient after edits. It must be paired with the series revision used to produce it. If expansion_revision != revision, the horizon is stale even if expansion_through_local is far in the future.
For destructive changes, keep immutable audit rows or an outbox/event log. That lets you reconstruct why an occurrence disappeared and safely notify downstream workers.

## PHP library choices

rlanvin/php-rrule is a lightweight PHP RRULE expander and states that it targets RFC 5545; it is appropriate for RRULE candidate generation, subject to verification of your exact version’s DST behavior and handling of RDATE/EXDATE as a complete recurrence set. Its own README notes that it differs from Python’s dateutil in RFC strictness, so build acceptance tests around your required semantics rather than assuming full iCalendar component handling.
Recommended implementation boundary:
- Parse/store the full recurrence model yourself: DTSTART, RRULE[], RDATE[], EXDATE[], timezone, duration, overrides.
- Delegate individual RRULE candidate generation to a library.
- Apply RFC set algebra, explicit DST fold/gap policy, exception reconciliation, and bounded range filtering in your domain layer.
- Run fixture tests around every zone transition relevant to customers, with a pinned tzdata container image/version.
If strict import/export interoperability is a core product requirement, prefer a PHP iCalendar component library that parses VTIMEZONE plus RRULE/RDATE/EXDATE together, and validate it against your DST and COUNT + EXDATE fixtures. If scheduling is internal and you control inputs, a narrow wrapper around php-rrule plus an explicit recurrence-set layer is easier to audit.

## Concurrency alternatives

- Recommended for most Laravel/PostgreSQL systems: SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the series row, bounded expansion, UNIQUE(series_id, recurrence_key), and INSERT … ON CONFLICT. It is simple, efficient, and gives clear ownership of the watermark.
- Advisory lock: use pg_advisory_xact_lock(hash(series_id)) if materialization spans several rows/tables or the master row may not exist yet. Still keep the unique index.
- Serializable transaction: use it when materialization enforces cross-series invariants, such as capacity, instructor/room conflicts, or a global booking limit. PostgreSQL can abort such transactions with SQLSTATE 40001; retry the entire transaction, not only the final insert.
- Queue partitioning: serialize jobs by series_id in the worker layer to reduce contention, but treat it as an optimization—not correctness. Retries, manual admin actions, and multiple deployment generations still require database constraints.
The key invariant is:
One logical recurrence identity per series may be materialized at most once, while its mutable projection—scheduled, cancelled, or overridden—may change transactionally.
That gives you RFC-compatible recurrence identity, deterministic DST handling, bounded storage/work, and retry-safe Laravel job execution.

Sources:
1. [datatracker.ietf](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5545)
2. [postgresql](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)
3. [github](https://github.com/rlanvin/php-rrule)
